title: Senior's toolkit: checking conditions
summary: Conditional breakpoints, the Immediate window, quick actions and table tests for logic you can trust.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: checking conditions
steps.body: A wrong condition hides in one case out of a thousand. Experienced developers stop exactly on that case, evaluate the condition live, and pin every case down in a table of tests.

toolkit.what: A breakpoint that only stops when an expression is true, so you land on the one bad case instead of pressing F5 a thousand times.
flags: right-click the red dot > Conditions, or Alt+F9 then C
right-click the gutter > Add Conditional Breakpoint
stop when the expression is true, e.g. `age < 0 && isMember`
(Visual Studio) stop when the value changes
toolkit.when: a rule misbehaves for some inputs only

toolkit.what: While stopped, type any expression and see its value at once. Split a long condition into its parts to find which one is false.
flags: (Visual Studio) print the value of an expression

toolkit.what: Quick actions on the current line. For logic, the useful ones are "Invert if", which flips a condition and swaps the branches correctly, and "Simplify conditional expression".
flags: rewrites `if (!a || !b) X else Y` as `if (a && b) Y else X`, applying De Morgan for you
turns `x != null && x.Length > 0` into a pattern
toolkit.example: Put the cursor on `if`, press Ctrl+., choose Invert if

toolkit.what: xUnit's table of test cases: one test method, one row per input. Perfect for a truth table: every combination becomes a row.
flags: the method runs once per data row
each row shows separately in the results, so you see which case failed

toolkit.what: Run only the tests you care about while you fix one rule.
flags: every test whose full name contains `Rules`
print each test and its output

toolkit.what: Patterns make range and null checks read like the rule they implement, and the compiler warns about cases that can never match.
flags: a null check that cannot be fooled by an overloaded `!=`
combine patterns without repeating the variable

steps.prompt: A discount rule is wrong for roughly 1 order in 5,000. The loop processes 20,000 orders and you know the bad ones have `Total > 500`. What is the fastest way to look at one?
options: A conditional breakpoint on the rule's line with the condition `order.Total > 500`
A normal breakpoint, then F5 until you reach a large order
Add `Console.WriteLine` for every order and read 20,000 lines
Rewrite the rule and hope the bug goes away
steps.explain: The condition is evaluated by the debugger on every pass, and it only stops on the case you care about. Then split the rule in the Immediate window to see which part is wrong.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to its job.
pairs: stop only on the one input that misbehaves
evaluate part of a condition while stopped
flip a condition and its branches safely
test every row of a truth table
rerun only the tests for one rule

steps.prompt: `&&` stops as soon as the answer is known. What does this print?
code: static bool Log(string name, bool value) { Console.Write(name); return value; }
bool a = Log("A", false) && Log("B", true);
bool b = Log("C", true) || Log("D", true);
steps.explain: `false && ...` is false whatever comes next, so B never runs. `true || ...` is true, so D never runs. Short-circuiting is why `user != null && user.IsAdmin` is safe.

steps.prompt: Complete the guard: throw when `percent` is below 0 or above 100.
steps.explain: `is < 0 or > 100` is a pattern: `or` combines two relational patterns. `||` would need the variable repeated, and `and` could never be true.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a rule fails for some inputs, do not reread it ten times: stop on the bad input with a conditional breakpoint and evaluate each part. Then write the case down as an `[InlineData]` row so it stays fixed. Let Ctrl+. do De Morgan for you when you flip a condition.
